blocks.text: Mendeleev left gaps in his 1869 table and predicted the properties of elements nobody had discovered. When gallium and germanium were found, they matched his predictions almost exactly. He could do this because the properties of elements repeat in a pattern — and that pattern is what this lesson is about.

blocks.markdown:
## The periodic law

The modern periodic law states that **the properties of the elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers**. Arrange elements by increasing atomic number and similar properties recur at regular intervals.

A **period** is a horizontal row. Across a period the number of occupied shells stays the same while nuclear charge rises by one each step.

A **group** is a vertical column. Down a group the number of outer electrons stays the same while a new shell is added each step.

blocks.title: The two forces that explain every trend
blocks.text: Effective nuclear charge is the net pull the nucleus exerts on an outer electron. It increases across a period because protons are added without adding a shell. Shielding is the screening effect of inner electrons, which increases down a group because extra full shells lie between the nucleus and the outer electrons.

rows: Rising nuclear charge pulls the same shells inward; new shells are added down a group
Outer electrons are held more tightly across, more loosely down

blocks.markdown:
### Ionisation energy

The **first ionisation energy** is the energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms:

M(g) -> M+(g) + e-

Successive ionisation energies always increase, because each electron is being pulled away from an increasingly positive ion. A **large jump** between successive values shows that an electron has just been removed from a shell closer to the nucleus — which tells you the group number.

blocks.title: Using successive ionisation energies to find the group
blocks.prompt: The first five ionisation energies of an element, in kJ per mole, are 578, 1817, 2745, 11577 and 14842. Which group does the element belong to?

steps.text: Look for the largest jump between consecutive values, not the largest value itself.
From 578 to 1817 is a factor of about 3, from 1817 to 2745 about 1.5, but from 2745 to 11577 is a factor of more than 4. That is the big jump.
The jump comes after the third electron is removed, so three electrons are relatively easy to take away and the fourth is very hard.
Those three easy electrons are the outer-shell electrons; the fourth comes from a full inner shell much nearer the nucleus.
Three outer electrons means group III. These values are in fact those of aluminium.

blocks.answer: Group III — the element is aluminium

blocks.markdown:
### Atomic radius versus ionic radius

- A **cation** is always smaller than its parent atom. Sodium loses its single third-shell electron, so Na+ has only two shells while Na has three.
- An **anion** is always larger than its parent atom. Chlorine gains an electron, increasing repulsion in the outer shell so the electron cloud expands.

For isoelectronic species, such as N3-, O2-, F-, Na+ and Mg2+, all with 10 electrons, radius falls as nuclear charge rises. So N3- is the largest and Mg2+ the smallest.

blocks.title: Always justify with charge and shielding
blocks.text: A bare statement such as 'atomic radius decreases across a period' scores one mark. Adding 'because nuclear charge increases while the electrons are added to the same shell, so the shells are pulled in more tightly' scores the rest. Name the cause every single time.

points: Properties of elements are a periodic function of atomic number.
Atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group.
Ionisation energy and electronegativity increase across a period and decrease down a group.
Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group.
A large jump in successive ionisation energies reveals the number of outer-shell electrons and hence the group.
Cations are smaller and anions larger than their parent atoms.
